newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Zambia's Chiluba takes oath of office for 2nd term.
newsitem.headline: Zambia's Chiluba takes oath of office for 2nd term.

text.p: Zambian President Frederick Chiluba was sworn in for a second term on Thursday after claiming victory in elections marred by an opposition boycott and a low turnout.
Election officials said results from 138 of the country's 150 constituencies gave Chiluba roughly 70 percent of the 1.19 million ballots counted.
Not all results were in by the time Chiluba took his oath of office in front of the country's most senior judge at the Supreme Court building in the capital.
Monday's poll was boycotted by major opposition parties, including that of main rival "Father of the Nation" Kenneth Kaunda.
Top brass from the country's army and police force attended the ceremony in their uniforms, while the dark-suited Chiluba swore to uphold the law of the land.

In a speech after taking his oath, Chiluba said the security forces would ensure there was no trouble in Zambia, where opposition supporters have demonstrated to protest what they saw as flawed polls.
"The army is...alert, and very alert, ready and willing to reinforce the police and air force," he said.
Chiluba's closest competitor in the presidential poll, Zambia Democratic Congress leader Dean Mungomba, took 144,366 votes.

The ruling Movement for Multi-party Democracy had been expected to win a decisive victory in the disputed election after seven opposition parties called on supporters to stay away from the polls, charging that the voting was rigged.

Two groups monitoring the election, however, gave conflicting views of the ballot. A Zambian group said the election was neither free nor fair since half of eligible voters were unfairly excluded but an international group said it found the balloting generally correct.
Political analysts and opposition figures said Chiluba's victory had been marred by the low turnout, which was partly due to the opposition's call for a boycott.
Half of Zambia's 4.6 million eligible voters were excluded from the rolls because of flawed registration.

Former president Kenneth Kaunda, who ruled from independence in 1964 until Chiluba trounced him in Zambia's first free polls in 1991, was barred from contesting the poll by a new law because his parents, from Malawi, were not Zambian.
Kaunda led the opposition boycott of the campaign and called for economic sanctions on Zambia.
